title: The Alarm Clock Moved Out of the Bedroom and the Bedroom Improved
body: For fifteen years my morning began the same way. The alarm inside my phone rang, I reached for the phone to silence it, and while the phone was already in my hand, warm and awake and pointed at my face, I checked everything. Weather, messages, one feed, another feed, a headline I would forget by breakfast. The day had a director before I had said a word to anyone in my own house. I want to report on the experiment that ended this, because the results were not subtle. The rule. The phone charges overnight in the kitchen, and a plain alarm clock, the kind with hands or with two aggressive bells, sits on the nightstand. That is the entire intervention. No app, no habit tracker, no subscription. The clock cost less than lunch. The first three mornings were honest about what the reaching had been. I woke, silenced the bell, and my hand kept going, patting the nightstand for the glass rectangle that was not there. The reaching was not for information. It was a reflex, the same way a dog goes to the door at the sound of a leash. Standing in the bedroom with nothing to scroll, I felt briefly abandoned, which taught me more about my habits than any screen-time report ever had. The measured changes after a month, kept honestly. I get out of bed maybe four minutes earlier, because there is no lying-in-place scrolling that stretches five minutes into twenty. The first half hour of the day contains no feed, which means the first thoughts of the day are my own thoughts, and it turns out they are less anxious than the imported ones. My partner reports that I say actual sentences before coffee now instead of grunting at a screen. And the phone, downstairs, holding nothing urgent, has stopped being the last thing I see at night, which improved falling asleep more than any advice about screens ever did, because the advice never removed the object, it only made me feel guilty while holding it. The objections deserve answers. What about emergencies? People knew where to reach me before phones had pockets, and the kitchen is eleven steps away; nothing has been lost but the ability to be interrupted by a group chat at midnight. What about the alarm app's gentle wake features? The two-bell clock wakes me completely; there is no snooze, because walking four steps to the clock would be pointless, snooze being a bedroom invention. What about checking the time at night? The clock has hands. Hands do not have notifications hiding behind them. The deeper finding is about ownership of the day's first decision. Every morning, the first thing I used to choose was chosen by an algorithm through a device I happened to be holding. Now the first thing I see is a clock and a window, and the first choice is mine, usually dull, always mine. Four minutes earlier, zero feeds before coffee, one kitchen that is now also a phone hotel. The ledger is not close. Move the phone out tonight. Any clock will do. The bedroom does not need a window into everything; it needs a bed, a window, and a bell that has no opinions.
